text:
Transit probability for a planet on a circular orbit seen from a random direction is, to very good approximation

P(transit) ≈ (R★ + Rp)/a ≃ R★ / a      (Rp ≪ R★ for Earth-like planets).

The stellar radii are stated to be equal, so the ratio of the two transit probabilities is set only by the ratio of their orbital semi–major axes:

P₁ / P₂ = a₂ / a₁ .

Use Kepler’s third law (a³ = GM★P²/4π² ⇒ a ∝ (M★)^{1/3} P^{2/3}):

a₂ / a₁ = (M₂ / M₁)^{1/3} (P₂ / P₁)^{2/3} .

Given data  
• P₂ = 3 P₁ (Planet 2’s period is three times longer)  
• M₁ = 2 M₂  (star of Planet 1 is twice the mass of star of Planet 2)

Hence

a₂ / a₁ = (M₂/M₁)^{1/3} (P₂/P₁)^{2/3}
         = (½)^{1/3} (3)^{2/3} .

Compute:

(½)^{1/3} ≈ 0.7937  
3^{2/3} = (3^{1/3})² ≈ (1.442)² ≈ 2.080.

Product: 0.7937 × 2.080 ≈ 1.65.

Therefore

P₁ / P₂ ≈ 1.65.

Planet 1 is about 1.65 times more likely to transit than Planet 2, so the observers should target Planet 1.

Answer: D
